newsitem.title: USA: Motorola seen benefiting from DRAM phaseout.
newsitem.headline: Motorola seen benefiting from DRAM phaseout.

text.p: Motorola Inc's plan to exit the DRAM (dynamic random access memory) semiconductor market will trim profits in the second quarter but will allow the company to focus on more profitable technology longer term.
"It's a good sign," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst with Gruntal & Co. "They're cleaning up the deck and focusing where they can really excel."

Motorola on Tuesday said it will take a second quarter $170 million pre-tax charge to phase out its participation in the DRAM market. The charge relates to the write-down of both technology development costs and manufacturing equipment.

A Motorola spokesman said the company would redirect resources into other memory technologies, such as its Fast Static Random Access Memory (FSRAM) where it is a leader and Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory (EEPROM).
"They seem to be moving in the right direction and focusing on the most profitable businesses," said Wojtek Uzdelewicz, an analyst for Cowen & Co.

The DRAM market is highly competitive, analysts said. DRAM products are mass produced by many manufacturers with little to distinguish them between brand names, and are thus treated as generic commodities in the marketplace.
Motorola said its share of the DRAM market has been less than two percent during the past two years and its DRAM business was not profitable in 1996.

Analysts pointed out that the company has not had a strong commitment to the market since the mid-1980s. Since then, it has participated mainly through joint ventures. DRAMs have been estimated to make up about five percent of the company's overall semiconductor business.
"You can't be a marginal player in a big market," Eraiba said. "It's a very competitive, commodity market."
Motorola said in the first stage of the phaseout it expects to end 16-megabit DRAM production at a Japanese joint-venture plant with Toshiba Corp by the end of this year.

Its production of 64-megabit DRAM at a Siemens AG joint venture plant now under construction in Virginia is expected to end in mid-2000, and Motorola's share of the manufacturing capacity there will be used to make FSRAM products.
Eric Buck, an analyst with Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette, said the change is not coming fast enough.

"The only thing they're doing in the near term is taking the write-off so they won't have the depreciation," Buck said, adding the elimination of the depreciation costs adds less than $0.01 a quarter to earnings per share estimates.
"It's disappointing they can't get out faster," Buck said.
Shares of Motorola slipped in early trading to 75-9/16 but were up 1/8 at 76-1/4 on Tuesday afternoon.
